title: The punctured spectrum of a Noetherian local ring is affine if and only if the dimension is at most one

standard_prerequisites.name: A Noetherian ring has finitely many minimal primes, and an element of the maximal ideal avoiding them can be chosen; the spectrum of a localisation is the corresponding open subset
standard_prerequisites.source_reference: Cited in the same chapter's algebra parent at proof lines 3358-3361 and reused at 3377-3379
standard_prerequisites.use: Produces the element f that makes the punctured spectrum a principal affine open in dimension one, and the nonzerodivisor used in the converse.

standard_prerequisites.name: Dimension drops by one on cutting out a nonzerodivisor, and a finite ring map induces a closed map on spectra
standard_prerequisites.source_reference: Cited at proof lines 3382-3383 and again at 3398-3400
standard_prerequisites.use: Gives the dimension count for A modulo fA and turns the finiteness of the ring map A/fA to B/fB into closedness of the induced map on spectra, which produces the contradiction.

standard_prerequisites.name: A module whose support is the closed point of a Noetherian local ring has finite length
standard_prerequisites.use: Makes the length l of the module of f-torsion in Q finite, which is what bounds the lengths of the modules Q[f^n].

core_obligations: Settle dimension zero and one in the affirmative direction: if the dimension is zero the punctured spectrum is empty and hence affine, and if the dimension is one one may choose an element of the maximal ideal avoiding the finitely many minimal primes, after which the punctured spectrum is the spectrum of the localisation at that element (proof lines 3356-3362).

Set up the converse: assume the punctured spectrum is the spectrum of a ring B, replace A by its reduced quotient (affineness and dimension are unaffected), and set Q = B/A; observe that Q is supported at the closed point and choose the same kind of nonzerodivisor f, which acts injectively on A, on B and hence on Q (proof lines 3364-3380).

Apply the snake lemma to multiplication by f on the short exact sequence with kernel A and quotient Q: this produces the four-term exact sequence displaying the module of f-torsion Q[f] as a subquotient of A/fA, which shows that Q[f] is a finite module, and hence of finite length l because its support is the closed point (proof lines 3381-3391).

Bound the lengths: let l_n be the length of the module of f^n-torsion in Q, show inductively that these lengths are finite and nondecreasing, then use the displayed exact sequence to show that the image of the f^n-torsion in the quotient of Q by f has length at most l; since Q is the union of its f^n-torsion modules, the length of the quotient of Q by f is bounded, so that quotient is finite (proof lines 3392-3396).

Conclude: the quotients by f give a finite ring map, whose induced map on spectra is therefore closed, while the spectrum of B modulo fB is exactly the punctured spectrum of the spectrum of A modulo fA; this is contradictory unless that punctured spectrum is empty, which says that the dimension of A modulo fA is zero, and with the dimension drop by one gives the claimed bound on the dimension of A (proof lines 3397-3405).
proof_roadmap: The positive direction is immediate in dimension zero and uses a well-chosen nonzerodivisor in dimension one (proof lines 3356-3362).

For the converse, reduce A to be reduced, compare the two rings through the quotient Q = B/A supported at the closed point, control the lengths of the f-power torsion modules of Q by the snake lemma, and finish with the closedness of the map on spectra induced by the finite ring map modulo f (proof lines 3364-3405).
difficulty_reason: The lemma determines exactly when the punctured spectrum of a Noetherian local ring is affine: it is affine precisely in dimension at most one (statement lines 3348-3353). The counted proof is a real argument of moderate length whose substance is in the converse: the author reduces to a reduced ring, forms the quotient Q = B/A supported at the closed point, applies the snake lemma to multiplication by a well-chosen nonzerodivisor to see that the f-torsion in Q is finite of finite length, propagates that bound by induction to the lengths of the f^n-torsion, concludes that the quotient of Q by f is finite, and then converts the resulting finite ring map modulo f into closedness on spectra, which contradicts the punctured spectrum being an open subset unless the dimension drops all the way to zero (proof lines 3364-3405). It is H2: the author explicitly calls the argument somewhat nonstandard, but every step is carried out in the counted span and the only inputs are standard commutative algebra, so no independent research-level claim is made.
